The same reason nearly we see behind nearly all ultimately failed industries (that weren't replaced by technology): corporate greed. When companies end up getting run by suits instead of creators, the suits try to mimic what is successful instead of finding their own niche. This cloning ultimately does little other than further cement the progenitor's place at the top by the imitators effectively destroying any alternative appeal they once had. They then blame their failures on the death of an industry as opposed to their murder of an industry and move on to try to clone the next big thing.

As applied to MMOS:

MMOs have always been attracting increasing numbers of casual users in spite of their hardcore nature. Activision Blizzard then took this and turned it into their primary demographic and had enormous success doing so. They streamlined their game and content and saw record breaking numbers for the west. Suddenly MMOs everywhere in the west began clamoring to also get their share of this appeal. Everything was getting dumbed down, simplified, and 'stream lined' left and right. Instead of having 50 MMOs each with their own little appeal you had WoW and 49 WoW clones.

WoW did what they did well and consequently the competition basically destroyed itself by trying to be WoW instead of carving out their own clear niches. However WoW positioned itself on a demographic that itself was inherently unstable and found themselves losing it as they moved onto the next big thing which is where we are today with WoW still on top of the western MMO market, yet most of their actual players being Asian marketshare scraps. People point to things like "I'd love to fail if that meant having 7 million players!" without realizing that 7 million players is now disproportionately made up of people paying literally the equivalent of pennies throughout Asia to play. It also lacks comparative context. WoW went from the top dog in gaming in the west to having 7 million players, primarily Asians paying next to nothing, while in that same time frame League of Legends went from an indie startup to about 70 million players a month and hundreds of millions in revenue.

It's just this really strange pattern you see repeated over and over. Somebody comes up with an innovative niche that does well. Tons of companies try to clone this success and fail at the expense of their own previous niches. As owner of original innovation gradually declines, entire industry falls to pieces. Ironically you can even see this behavior from Activision Blizzard now. Once they saw League of Legends was crushing them they decided to start their own MOBA but they didn't actually offer anything particularly unique other than "Kind of like League of Legends, but not!" The casualization of the genre is an impetus towards improvement. Here's the deal, a game developer makes a game, let's say in this case an MMORPG. Now, an MMORPG is what you would call a 'niche' game, they're not normally AAA funded and supported by the gaming community at large, in fact many previous to World of Warcraft were flops (looking at you, Final Fantasy 11). They simply don't appeal to 100% of gamers, never have, and never really will.

Now WoW came out, and that one was a game-changer. People loved it. This is one that actually appealed to the masses. This is sort of a genre-breaking trend so to speak, and many other games came out later trying to ride the WoW bandwagon (hence, all the titles you listed). The problem being, RPGs are niche to begin with, and only going to appeal to RPG gamers specifically (you typically won't find a lot of Call of Duty fans espousing about the next great RPG on their forums, and nor would you expect them to), but game developers don't like only appealing to the specific niche, so they simplify the games in order to appeal to more and more of the overall gaming demographic while simultaneously moving away from the RPG niche that was originally appealing in the first place. Other titles began popping up around this time, Knights of the Old Republic made an MMORPG, and several others began being released. Some were more geared towards being towards the original RPG elements, and others more towards an action RPG according to their own various styles. This saturated the market, gamers who were tired of WoW and looking for something different to replace it had a plethora of options and began taking those on, but quickly lost interest and went back to WoW or started going into other games altogether.

One of the best examples of this would be Shining Force. This was a pioneer of what later became called 'Tactical RPGs' (other games in a similar vein that came out would be Warsong, Final Fantasy Tactics, Tactics Ogre, or X-Com). This was one of the creators of the entire genre, but as such, fell into the niche of not achieving commercial success like other games at the time like Sonic the HedgeHog. As such, after they made Shining Force 2, which was exponentially better than the original, they went on to make a normal RPG called 'Shining in the Dark', which, unfortunately, really fucking sucked. They tried their hand at a few other genres and abandoned the tactical RPG altogether in order to try and achieve bigger success but in doing so, alienated their existing customer base and gained almost no new customer base to replace them, and the company subsequently folded after a few failed attempts.

I don't fully understand why gaming developers can't just make a great game inside of their niche, make their money back plus profit, and just be happy with that instead of constantly trying to dumb their games down to appeal to the masses so their game can sell like Call of Duty. The truth of the matter is many of the absolute best games are undeniably inside of their niche, and for a solid experience in that niche you'll start looking for the best of the best--which are games that are not meant to be universally appealing, but rather appeal to people inside of that genre. The best Grand Strategy Games are games that the strong majority of gamers have absolutely never heard of (Europa IV, Crusader Kings 2, etc.). Many genres are like that, truly.
